# TEB3 board data

Inputs for `teb_mcp.netlist`. Board topology, not credentials - but see the
note on the BOM before committing anything here.

## Provenance

Both files came from Eran Raz by mail, "TEB3 Rev C BOM and netlist".

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `TEB3_Rev_C_netlist_290926.txt` | Cadence Allegro 23.1 "Telesis" netlist |
| `TEB3_Rev_C_BOM_290926_2.xlsx` | Bill of materials |

The netlist header records its own source:

```
(FOR DRAWING: H:/TEB3/export for AI/TEB3_Revc_upadated.brd)
(GENERATED BY: ALLEGRO 23.1 S002 (4170606))
(Tue Sep 29 14:43:06 2026)
```

**The netlist is Rev C.** A board of a different revision may be wired
differently, so confirm the physical board before trusting a pin lookup.

## Why the file lives here

`netlist.py` defaults to this path. The alternative - pointing at whatever is
currently in someone's Downloads folder - breaks silently the first time that
folder is cleared, and a pin map that silently becomes empty is worse than one
that is obviously absent. `TEB_NETLIST` overrides the path.

## Format

Sections are introduced by a `$` line. Each marker appears **twice**: once for
the data, and again later paired with `$A_PROPERTIES` for per-object
properties. Only the first `$NETS` is the net list.

```
$PACKAGES
<part> ! <footprint> ! <device> ; REFDES REFDES ...
$NETS
NETNAME ; REFDES.PIN REFDES.PIN ...
```

A trailing `,` continues a record onto the next indented line. Any token may be
single-quoted when it contains characters Allegro treats as special.

## The connector mapping — READ THIS BEFORE TRUSTING A SYMBOL

There are **two** numbering schemes here, and conflating them is the trap.

**Solid — net name to connector pin.** The netlist says the net `GPIO_B6`
touches `J8` pin 6. Lookups by location (`pin_net(pin="J8.6")`) or by net name
are read straight out of `$NETS` and are trustworthy.

| Net family | Refdes |
|---|---|
| `GPIO_A*` | `J7` |
| `GPIO_B*` | `J8` (even pins only; odd are `POWER_OUT0..7` / `ID0..6`) |
| `GPIO_C*` | `J12` |
| `GPIO_D*` | `J14` |
| `GPIO_E*` | `J24` |
| `GPIO_G*` | `J21` |
| `ANALOG_INPUTS*` / `ANALOG_OUTPUTS*` | `J22` |
| `FPGA_BANK3_*` | `J13` |

**Not established — `TebConnector.h` symbol to net.** An earlier version of
this file claimed the header symbol `GPIO_B06` (value 1106) was the net
`GPIO_B6`, "verified by 239 index matches with zero mismatches".

**That check was circular and proved nothing.** The board names each net after
the connector pin it lands on, so of course the index in `GPIO_B6` equals pin 6.
Matching it to `GPIO_B06` was pure name equality.

Evidence that the join is actually wrong:

- `EC/Common/Boards/SVB/SVB_Akko.cpp` drives `_TEB_GPIO_B01`, `B03`, `B05` …
  `B17` — **odd** indices. J8's odd pins carry `POWER_OUT` and `ID` nets, not
  GPIO. Those symbols cannot be odd J8 pins.
- `EC/Common/Boards/SVB/SVB_Ramon.cpp` maps **286 pins across TEB I/F 1–8**
  (`GPIO_101..GPIO_8xx`) and runs on this very board (`board_generation=3`,
  composition `Ramon/1.2`). An earlier claim here that I/F 1–9 were "not on the
  TEB3 board" is **false**.

Confirmed empirically: driving `GPIO_B06` (1106) as output-high produced
**0.00 V** on J8 pin 6 at the multimeter, while the FPGA was demonstrably alive
(register reads returned real data).

The header's letter families and the board's net-name letters are most likely
two unrelated schemes sharing a prefix. Until that is settled, **prefer
connector-location lookups**, and treat any symbol lookup as a hint.

### How to settle it

Drive one candidate symbol at a time and measure the connector pin — for J8
pin 6 the candidates are `GPIO_106`, `206`, `306`, `406`, `506`, `606`, `706`,
`806` — or get the TEB3 schematic sheet that labels each QSS-025 header with
its TEB I/F number.

## Committing

The netlist is safe board topology. **Review the BOM before committing it** -
BOMs often carry supplier names and pricing.
